concepts.title: European Traders Arrive: The Portuguese
concepts.definition: The sea route to India brought European traders to Indian shores at the end of the fifteenth century, with the Portuguese among the first to set up trading posts and forts on the coasts, opening the chapter of European rivalry for Indian trade.
concepts.key_idea: Ocean routes turned India into a stage for European commercial rivalry.
concepts.textbook_ref: hees102.txt lines 1-155 (arrival of the Portuguese in India)
question_patterns: who were the first Europeans to reach India by sea and when
why did European trading companies come to India
where did the Portuguese set up their trading centres in India
how did the discovery of a sea route change India's trade
name the European powers that competed for trade in India
what made Indian coasts attractive to foreign traders

solution_steps.explain: The Cape route around Africa connected Europe directly to India.
Portuguese came first, followed by Dutch, English and French traders.
Fortified trading posts on the coasts began as commerce and grew into power.

concepts.title: The Delhi Sultanate and Its Resistance
concepts.definition: From the thirteenth century the Delhi Sultanate ruled large parts of north India through dynasties like the Tughlaqs and Lodis, but its power faced constant resistance from regional kingdoms, and southern powers such as the Vijayanagara Empire stayed outside its grip.
concepts.key_idea: Sultanate control stretched far but never unopposed - regional powers pushed back.
concepts.textbook_ref: hees102.txt lines 155-510 (sultanate dynasties, resistance, Tughlaq and Lodi extents)
question_patterns: name the dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in order
how did regional kingdoms resist the Delhi Sultanate
why did the Tughlaq empire begin to break up
what was the extent of the Lodi dynasty
describe the resistance to the Delhi Sultanate in the south
why is the period called one of reshaping the political map

solution_steps.explain: Follow the succession of sultanate dynasties and their shifting territories.
Provincial governors and southern kingdoms repeatedly challenged Delhi's authority.
Empires like Vijayanagara kept the deep south independent of sultanate rule.

concepts.title: The Vijayanagara Empire
concepts.definition: Founded in the fourteenth century in the Deccan, the Vijayanagara Empire grew into a powerful Hindu kingdom famous for its wealth, trade and the city of Hampi, standing as a major counterforce to the sultanates of the north.
concepts.key_idea: Vijayanagara anchored southern power against northern expansion.
question_patterns: who founded the Vijayanagara empire and when
why was the city of Vijayanagara famous
how did Vijayanagara resist the northern sultanates
what made Hampi a prosperous city
which rivers and regions came under Vijayanagara
describe the political role of Vijayanagara in the Deccan

solution_steps.explain: Brothers of the Sangama line established the kingdom in the mid-1300s.
Trade in spices, cloth and gems enriched the capital at Hampi.
Wars with the Bahmani sultans and later Deccan powers shaped the region.

concepts.title: Rajputs, Hoysalas and Regional Kingdoms
concepts.definition: Beyond the big empires, the political map was studded with regional kingdoms - Rajput houses in the north and west, the Hoysalas in the south, the Eastern Gangas in Odisha - each building temples, trade and armies and adding their patches to India's changing map.
concepts.key_idea: Many strong regional kingdoms, not one power, made the medieval political map.
concepts.textbook_ref: hees102.txt lines 155-165 (Eastern Ganga and Hoysala territories), 390-445
question_patterns: name two regional kingdoms that flourished alongside the sultanate
where did the Hoysala kingdom rule
what were the achievements of the Eastern Ganga kingdom
how did Rajput kingdoms maintain their independence
why did regional powers flourish during this period
show how the political map changed between 1300 and 1500

solution_steps.explain: Place the Rajput states, Hoysalas and Gangas on the map.
Temples, trade routes and hill forts anchored their power.
Wars and alliances redrew boundaries from one century to the next.
